10 [[Big Ten Conference|Western / Big Ten]] (1901–1904, 1906, 1918, 1922–1923, 1925–1926) | awards = | coaching_records = | CFBHOF_year = 1951 | CFBHOF_id = 1235 }} '''Fielding Harris Yost''' ({{IPAc-en|j|oʊ|s|t}}; April 30, 1871 – August 20, 1946) was an American [[college football]] player, coach and athletics administrator. He served as the head football coach at [[Ohio Wesleyan University]], the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|University of Nebraska]], the [[University of Kansas]], [[Stanford University]], [[San Jose State University]], and the [[University of Michigan]], compiling a coaching career record of 198–35–12. During his 25 seasons as the head football coach at [[Ann Arbor, Michigan|Ann Arbor]], Yost's [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]] won six [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championships]], captured ten [[Big Ten Conference]] titles, and amassed a record of 165–29–10. From 1901 to 1905, his "Point-a-Minute" squads had a record of 55–1–1, outscoring their opponents by a margin of 2,821–42. The [[1901 Michigan Wolverines football team|1901 team]] beat [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford]], 49–0, in the [[1902 Rose Bowl]], the first college football [[bowl game]]. Under Yost, Michigan won four straight national championships from 1901 to 1904 and two more in 1918 and 1923. In 1921, Yost became Michigan's [[athletic director]] and served in that capacity until 1940. He was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] as a coach in 1951.{{cite web|url=http://www.cfbhall.com/inductees/?ps=true&playername=Fielding+Yost&fromDate=&toDate=&school=&yearInducted=&position=&submit=Search|title=Hall of Fame Inductees|publisher=Atlanta Hall Management, Inc.|access-date=July 27, 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817090639/http://www.cfbhall.com/inductees/?ps=true&playername=Fielding+Yost&fromDate=&toDate=&school=&yearInducted=&position=&submit=Search|archive-date=August 17, 2016}} Yost was also a successful businessman, lawyer, and author; but he is best known as a leading figure in pioneering the development of college football into a national phenomenon. ==Early life== Yost was born in [[Fairview, West Virginia]], in April 1871. Yost's family had settled in West Virginia, in 1825. He was the oldest of four children of Parmenus (sometimes Permenus) Wesley Yost and Elzena Jane (Ammons) Yost, both of West Virginia. His father was a farmer and a Confederate veteran.{{Harvnb|Falls|1996|page=19}} His family had been in Fairview since 1825 when his second great grandfather, David Yost, settled there and took up a grant of over 2,000 acres.{{Harvnb|Behee|1971|page=17}} Yost was educated in the local schools and became a deputy marshal in Fairview as a teenager.{{Harvnb|Onofrio|1999|pages=289–290}} At seventeen, he earned a public-school teaching certificate.{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=312}} ==College== [[File:WVU football team 1895.jpg|thumb|[[1895 West Virginia Mountaineers football team]], with Yost seated the furthest-right in the middle row]] Yost began his college education at [[Fairmont State University|Fairmont Normal School]] in [[Fairmont, West Virginia]]. He then taught school at [[Patterson Creek, West Virginia]], during the 1889–90 school year. He next enrolled at the Ohio Normal School (now known as [[Ohio Northern University]]). Yost played for the Ohio Normal baseball team.{{cite news|title=Fielding Yost Will Write On Football For The Gazette Sports Page Readers|newspaper=Charleston Gazette|date=September 27, 1931}} After three years at Ohio Normal, he returned to West Virginia to work in the oil fields. In 1895, Yost enrolled at [[West Virginia University]] where he studied law, earning an [[LL.B.]] He also played football for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football team]].[http://www.dailymail.com/Sports/WVUSports/200712180207 Maramba, Kris Wise, "Fielding Yost, another son of Marion County, excelled with Wolverines"], ''[[Charleston Daily Mail]]'', December 18, 2007 {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20071220045302/http://www.dailymail.com/Sports/WVUSports/200712180207 |date=December 20, 2007 }} A 6-foot, 200 pounder, Yost was a standout at [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|tackle]] at West Virginia into the 1896 season. ===Joining Lafayette=== [[File:Fielding Yost and teammate c 1895 or 1896.jpg|thumb|right|Yost (left) with a teammate c 1895 or 1896]] In October 1896, after his team lost three home games to [[1896 Lafayette football team|Lafayette]], played on three different fields over the course of three days,{{cite news|url=http://imago.lafayette.edu/cdm4/document.php?CISOROOT=/lafayette&CISOPTR=17092&CISOSHOW=17088&REC=2|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20120216055621/http://cdm.lafayette.edu/?CISOROOT=/lafayette&CISOPTR=17092&CISOSHOW=17088&REC=2|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 16, 2012|title=Lafayette vs. University of West Virginia|work=The Lafayette|page=36|date=October 23, 1896}} he transferred in mid-season to join Coach [[Parke H. Davis]]'s national championship team at Lafayette. Just a week after playing ''against'' Davis in West Virginia, Yost was playing ''for'' Davis in Lafayette's historic 6–4 win over the [[1896 Penn Quakers football team|Penn Quakers]]. The fortuitous timing of his appearance on the Lafayette roster did not go unnoticed by Penn officials. They called it "the Yost affair." The [[Public Ledger (Philadelphia)|Philadelphia ''Ledger'']] quoted Yost as saying that he came to Lafayette only to play football. The fact that he appeared in a Lafayette uniform only once, in the Penn game,{{cite news|url=http://imago.lafayette.edu/cdm4/document.php?CISOROOT=/lafayette&CISOPTR=20210&CISOSHOW=20202&REC=1|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20120216055641/http://cdm.lafayette.edu/?CISOROOT=/lafayette&CISOPTR=20210&CISOSHOW=20202&REC=1|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 16, 2012|title=Lafayette College Foot-Ball.|work=The Lafayette|page=100|date=January 15, 1897 }} and that he returned to West Virginia within two weeks of the contest did not help appearances. He assured all concerned that he would return to Lafayette for at least three years of study.{{cite news|url=http://imago.lafayette.edu/cdm4/document.php?CISOROOT=/lafayette&CISOPTR=24180&CISOSHOW=24173&REC=4|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20120216055627/http://cdm.lafayette.edu/?CISOROOT=/lafayette&CISOPTR=24180&CISOSHOW=24173&REC=4|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 16, 2012|title=Editorial Department and Yost a Bona-fide Student|work=The Lafayette|pages=66–68|date=November 20, 1896}} ==Coaching career== ===Ohio Wesleyan=== Yost began his coaching career at age 26 as head coach of the [[1897 Ohio Wesleyan football team]]. Yost's team compiled a 7–1–1 record, shut out six of its nine opponents (including a 6–0 victory over [[1897 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]] and a scoreless tie with [[1897 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]]), and outscored all opponents by a total of 144 to 32. Yost played at left tackle against Michigan, leading to a protest that Ohio Wesleyan had assured Michigan that Yost, a paid coach and non-student, would not play and had engaged in trickery by introducing another individual as Yost. One week later, Michigan announced that it would no longer schedule games against Ohio Wesleyan.{{cite news|title=Michigan Blacklists Ohio Wesleyan|newspaper=The Saint Paul Globe|date=October 17, 1897|page=14|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3017365/michigan_blacklists_ohio_wesleyan/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}{{cite news|title=Michigan Plays a Poor Game: Fails to Score Against Ohio Wesleyan's Eleven|newspaper=The Daily Inter Ocean|date=October 10, 1897|page=8|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3017360/michigan_plays_a_poor_game/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}} ===Nebraska=== In 1898, Yost was hired to coach the [[1898 Nebraska Bugeaters football team|Nebraska football team]] with compensation of $1,000 for 10 weeks of service.{{cite news|title=Football|newspaper=Wheeling (WV) Daily Intelligencer|date=September 5, 1898|page=3|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8535550/football_fielding_yost/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202024039/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8535550/football_fielding_yost/|archive-date=February 2, 2017}} The 1898 Nebraska team compiled an 8–3 record, including victories over Iowa State (23–10), Missouri (47–6), Kansas (18–6), and Colorado (23–10), and losses to Drake (6–5) and Iowa (6–5). ===Kansas=== In June 1899, the University of Kansas Athletic Association offered Yost $350, and an additional $150 conditionally, to coach the school's football team.{{cite news|title=Probable Football Coach: Yost of Nebraska Likely To Be Employed in That Capacity|newspaper=Lawrence Daily Journal|date=June 7, 1899|page=4|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/2989027/probable_football_coach/}} After spending the summer in Colorado, Yost arrived in [[Lawrence, Kansas]], on September 4, 1899.{{cite news|title=Coach Yost On Hand|newspaper=Lawrence Daily World|date=September 5, 1899|page=4|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8535521/coach_yost_on_hand/}} During the 1899 season, the Kansas football team "lived separate from the rest of the students and ate specially selected and prepared food . . . with Coach Yost as their only mentor".{{cite news|title=Will Yost Coach Tigers?|newspaper=Larence Daily World|date=December 4, 1899|page=2|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8535527/will_yost_coach_tigers/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202024248/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8535527/will_yost_coach_tigers/|archive-date=February 2, 2017}} The team compiled an undefeated 10–0 record, outscoring opponents 280–37. The season included victories over the Haskell Indians (12–0 and 18–0), Nebraska (36–20), and Missouri (34–6). During the 1899–1900 academic year, Kansas had Yost as its football coach and [[James Naismith]] as its basketball coach. Naismith also served as an assistant football coach during the 1899 season. ===Stanford=== In May 1900, Yost was hired as the football coach at [[Stanford University]],{{cite news|title=Likes Yost's Manner: President Jordan of Leland Stanford University Gives His Opinion of the Coach|newspaper=Lawrence Daily Journal|date=May 8, 1900|page=4|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/2989072/likes_yosts_manner/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151119230747/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/2989072/likes_yosts_manner/|archive-date=November 19, 2015}} and, after traveling home to West Virginia, he arrived in [[Palo Alto, California]], on August 21, 1900.{{cite news|title=Stanford's Football Coach Has Arrived|newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle|date=August 22, 1900|page=4|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/27618966/?terms=yost%2Bstanford%2Bfootball}} Yost led the 1900 Stanford team to a 7–2–1, outscoring opponents 154–20. ===Michigan=== {{Main|History of Michigan Wolverines football in the Yost era}} [[File:Fielding Yost 1915.png|thumb|Yost from the 1915 ''Michiganensian'']] After first applying at Illinois,{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=313}} Yost was hired in 1901 by [[Charles A. Baird]] as the head football coach for the [[Michigan Wolverines football]] team.{{cite news|title=Yost Takes Charge at Michigan|newspaper=Detroit Free Press|date=April 6, 1901|page=6|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/6640339/yost_takes_charge_at_michigan/}} Yost coached at Michigan from 1901 through 1923, and again in 1925 and 1926. He was highly successful at Michigan, winning 165 games, losing only 29, and tying 10 for a winning percentage of .833. Under Yost, Michigan won four straight [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championships]] from 1901 to 1904 and two more in 1918 and 1923. ====Point-a-minute==== Yost's first [[1901 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan team in 1901]] outscored its opposition by a margin of 550–0 en route to a perfect season and victory in the [[1902 Rose Bowl|inaugural Rose Bowl]] on January 1, 1902, over [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford]], the team Yost had coached the year before. From 1901 to 1904, Michigan did not lose a game, and was tied only once in a legendary game with the [[Minnesota Golden Gophers football|Minnesota Golden Gophers]] that led to the establishment of the [[Little Brown Jug (college football trophy)|Little Brown Jug]] trophy. Yost's teams used the [[short punt formation]].Retyl, Richard, [http://www.mgoblue.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/110910aaa.html U-M's Shotgun Offense is Older than the Winged Helmets Themselves] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101113070511/http://www.mgoblue.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/110910aaa.html |date=November 13, 2010 }}. November 9, 2010. MGoBlue.com. Retrieved June 26, 2013. He also developed a play called "Old 83" resembling an [[Option offense|option]].{{Harvnb|Pope|1955|page=315}} Before Michigan finally lost a game to [[Amos Alonzo Stagg]]'s [[Chicago Maroons football|Chicago Maroons]] squad at the end of the 1905 season, they had gone 56 straight games without a defeat, the second longest such streak in college football history. During their first five seasons under Yost, Michigan outscored its opponents 2,821–42,{{cite web |url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/misc/fbrecord.htm |title=All-Time University of Michigan Football Record |publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library |access-date=March 27, 2011}} earning the Michigan team the nickname "Point-a-Minute."{{Harvnb|Gruver|2002|page=21}} The team featured running back [[Willie Heston]], who Yost called the greatest player he ever saw.{{cite news|author=Grantland Rice (repeating comments made by Fielding Yost)|title=In the Sportlight|newspaper=Ogden Standard-Examiner|date=January 10, 1925}}{{refn|group=n|Yost's all-time All-America [[backfield]] was Heston, [[Walter Eckersall]], [[Jim Thorpe]], and [[Elmer Oliphant]].{{Harvnb|Wheeler|2012|page=198}}}} In 1904, [[Germany Schulz]] stood up from the center position and created the position of [[linebacker]]. Yost was horrified at first, but came to see the wisdom in Schulz's innovation.Malcolm Bingay, "A Little About This and That: How Schulz Entered Michigan Still A Mystery," ''The Morning Herald'', May 1, 1951; "Frankly Speaking: Schulz' Great Grid Exploits Reviewed," ''The Long Beach Press-Telegram'', April 17, 1951. ====Independent==== In 1906, Michigan president [[James Burrill Angell]] called for a series of conference meetings to further regulate football, leading to new rules such as limiting football teams to no more than five games and players to three years of eligibility.{{cite book| title=The University of Michigan, an encyclopedic survey ... Wilfred B. Shaw, editor | date=1941 |url=https://quod.lib.umich.edu/u/umsurvey/AAS3302.0004.001/1:3.4.1?rgn=div3;view=fulltext}} One of the new rules would require the football coach to be a full-time employee of the university, leading to Yost's opposition to the changes. Ultimately Yost won out and convinced Michigan's board to support him over Angell and against the conference.{{cite book| last1=Duderstadt | first1=James J. | title=Intercollegiate Athletics and the American University: A University President's Perspective | date=4 September 2003 | publisher=University of Michigan Press | isbn=0-472-08943-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tEg_DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA232}} In April 1907, Michigan was voted out of the conference for refusing to adhere to the new league rules.{{cite news| url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1907/04/14/106748007.pdf | work=The New York Times | title=CONFERENCE OUSTS MICHIGAN; Severs Relations with University for Non-Observance of Rules | date=April 14, 1907}} In 1908, Michigan lost to Penn 29–0, the worst defeat suffered by a Michigan team during the Yost era.{{cite news|author=Joe Jackson|title=Michigan's Worst Defeat of the Yost Regime: Figures in Pennsylvania Game Are 29 to 0, Men of the East Proving Best Eleven School Has Had Against Michigan--Injuries To Schulz and Allerdice Prove Costly|newspaper=Detroit Free Press|date=November 15, 1908|page=17|url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/freep/access/1743286352.html?FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:AI&type=historic&date=Nov+15%2C+1908&author=JOE+JACKSON&pub=Detroit+Free+Press+(1858-1922)&edition=&startpage=17&desc=MICHIGAN%27S+WORST+DEFEAT+OF+THE+YOST+REGIME|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130131171613/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/freep/access/1743286352.html?FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:AI&type=historic&date=Nov+15,+1908&author=JOE+JACKSON&pub=Detroit+Free+Press+(1858-1922)&edition=&startpage=17&desc=MICHIGAN'S+WORST+DEFEAT+OF+THE+YOST+REGIME|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 31, 2013}} Yost said of Schulz's performance: "He gave the greatest one-man exhibition of courage I ever saw on a football field."{{cite web|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fballam/aaschulz.htm|publisher=The Regents of the University of Michigan|title=University of Michigan Football All-American, 1907, Team Captain, 1908; Adolph "Germany" Schulz|access-date=December 31, 2007|date=February 10, 2007|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071218082000/http://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fballam/aaschulz.htm|archive-date=December 18, 2007}} In 1909, Michigan suffered its first loss to [[1909 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]].{{cite web|title=1909 Football Team|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1909fbt.htm|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100408090313/http://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1909fbt.htm|archive-date=April 8, 2010}} In 1910, Michigan was led by All-Americans [[Albert Benbrook]] and [[Stanfield Wells]] and played its only undefeated season of the independent years, compiling a 3–0–3 record.{{cite web|title=1910 Football Team|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1910fbt.htm|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090611052233/http://www.bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1910fbt.htm|archive-date=June 11, 2009}} In 1916, [[John Maulbetsch]] led Michigan to one of its finest records. The Wolverines won seven straight games. ====Return to Western Conference==== [[File:Fielding H. Yost 1928.jpg|thumb|180px|Yost from the 1928 ''Michiganensian'']] Led by fullback [[Frank Steketee]], the 1918 team went undefeated in the war-shortened season. The [[1922 Michigan Wolverines football team|1922]] and [[1923 Michigan Wolverines football team|1923]] teams went undefeated, led by punter [[Harry Kipke]]. The only blemish was a [[1922 Michigan vs. Vanderbilt football game|tie]] with Yost protege and brother-in-law [[Dan McGugin]]'s [[1922 Vanderbilt Commodores football team|Vanderbilt]].{{refn|group=n|Yost was best man at McGugin's wedding.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/6939550/the_atlanta_constitution/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009181155/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/6939550/the_atlanta_constitution/|archive-date=October 9, 2016|work=The Atlanta Constitution|page=3|date=December 3, 1905|access-date=October 8, 2016|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|title=Coach McGugin to Wed}} {{Open access}}}} At the end of the season, Yost called the 1925 Michigan team "the greatest football team I ever coached" and "the greatest football team I ever saw in action".{{cite news|title=Yost Calls 1925 Eleven Greatest: Does Not Even Except Wonderful Teams of 1901 and 1902; Rolled Up Grand 227 Point Total; Wolverine Mentor Says He's Proud to Have Coached Boys|newspaper=The Hartford Courant|page=B2|date=November 29, 1925|url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/courant/access/807449222.html?dids=807449222:807449222&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:AI&type=historic&date=Nov+29%2C+1925&author=&pub=Hartford+Courant&desc=YOST+CALLS+1925+ELEVEN+GREATEST&pqatl=google|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130131192524/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/courant/access/807449222.html?dids=807449222:807449222&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:AI&type=historic&date=Nov+29,+1925&author=&pub=Hartford+Courant&desc=YOST+CALLS+1925+ELEVEN+GREATEST&pqatl=google|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 31, 2013}} The team featured quarterback [[Benny Friedman]] and left end [[Bennie Oosterbaan]], sometimes referred to as "The Benny-to-Bennie Show". In tribute to the school where Yost began his coaching career, he arranged for Michigan to play its first game at [[Ferry Field]] (September 30, 1905) and its [[1927 Michigan Wolverines football team#Week 1: Ohio Wesleyan|first game]] at [[Michigan Stadium]] (October 1, 1927) against Ohio Wesleyan.{{cite web|title=The Michigan Stadium Story: Opening Day, Oct. 1, 1927, UM vs. Ohio|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library|access-date=August 10, 2015|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/stadium/stadtext/openday.htm|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150816113430/http://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/stadium/stadtext/openday.htm|archive-date=August 16, 2015}} ==Athletic director== [[File:Fielding Yost, UM Football, ca. 1938.jpg|left|thumb|194x194px|Yost {{Circa|1938}}]] After retiring from coaching, Yost remained at Michigan as the school's [[athletic director]], a position he held until 1940, then held the title of athletic director emeritus. Under his leadership, [[Michigan Stadium]], Yost Fieldhouse (now [[Yost Ice Arena]]), and the university's golf course were constructed. ==Later years and death== [[File:Fielding Yost grave Forest Hill Cemetery.JPG|thumb|right|Yost's grave]] Yost was in poor health for several years before his death and was hospitalized at the [[Battle Creek Sanitarium]] in May 1946.{{cite news |title=Fielding Yost Sick |newspaper=[[The Herald-Mail|The Morning Herald]] |location=[[Hagerstown, Maryland]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=May 31, 1946 }} He reportedly suffered from a stroke, but was released after two weeks and returned to his home in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]].{{cite news |title=Fielding Yost Said To Be Seriously Ill |newspaper=[[Ironwood Daily Globe]] |location=[[Ironwood, Michigan]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=May 31, 1946 }} In August 1946, Yost died of a [[biliary colic|gall bladder attack]] at his home. He was survived by his wife, whom he had married in 1906, a son, Fielding H. Yost, Jr., two brothers, Ellis and Nicholas, and a sister, Mrs. Charles Barry.{{cite news |title=Yost, Michigan's Famed Coach, Dies at 75: Point a Minute Team Highlight of Long Career|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune|Chicago Daily Tribune]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=August 21, 1946 |page=29 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/129423414/|via=Newspapers.com}} Yost was buried at Ann Arbor's [[Forest Hill Cemetery (Ann Arbor, Michigan)|Forest Hill Cemetery]] near the University of Michigan campus.{{cite news |title=Fielding Yost Laid To Rest Near Campus |newspaper=[[Abilene Reporter-News]] |location=[[Abilene, Texas]] |date=August 23, 1946 }} ==Personal== A native of West Virginia, Yost's unusual pronunciation of the school's name, "MEE-she-gan," copied by long-time Michigan football broadcaster [[Bob Ufer]], is affectionately carried on by many Michigan football fans and often referenced by [[ESPN]] sportscaster [[Chris Fowler]]. A devout [[Christians|Christian]], he was among the first coaches to allow [[Jewish]] players on his teams, including [[Joe Magidsohn]] and [[Benny Friedman]]. However, [[Murray Sperber]]'s book ''Shake Down the Thunder'' places principal responsibility for the Big Ten blackballing and boycotting of Notre Dame on Yost. It also claims this was motivated by anti-Catholic and anti-immigrant prejudice common in the early 20th century, though John Kyrk's book ''Natural Enemies'' points out that there was a bitter feud between Yost and [[Knute Rockne]], head coach of the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame football team]]. ==Legacy== Yost had a profound impact on the Michigan athletics department. "No other man has ever given as much heart, soul, brains, and tongue to the game he loved—football" said [[Grantland Rice]].{{Harvnb|Chengelis|2012|page=41}} A longtime football coach and athletic director, his career was marked with achievement. Yost was among the inaugural class of inductees to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 1951. [[Tommy Hughitt]] was heavily inspired by Yost's system and used it to great success,{{cite news|title=Alumni Notes|year=1915|publisher=The Michigan technic, Volumes 28-29|page=231|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-U3iAAAAMAAJ&q=hughitt+maine+football&pg=RA1-PA231}} later adapting it to the professional game with the [[Youngstown Patricians]] and [[Buffalo (NFL)|Buffalo All-Americans]]. The [[Yost Ice Arena]], the home venue of the [[Michigan Wolverines men's ice hockey]], was named in his honor. In 2021, a committee commissioned by the University of Michigan president recommended that the school remove Yost's name from its ice hockey arena, citing a history of racial issues involving the former football coach and athletic director University of Michigan conducted an in-depth review of his career and concluded in 2021 that Yost had a "profoundly deep and negative impact on people of color" through active discrimination and upholding a segregated athletic environment. Baird|Charles Baird]]; invented the fieldhouse concept that bears his name; and supervised the building of the first on-campus building dedicated to intramural sports.{{Harvnb|Chengelis|2012|page=40}} ====Hurry up==== Yost was also known for a series of admonitions to his players beginning with the words, "Hurry up," for example, "Hurry up and be the first man down the field on a punt or kick-off." This inclination earned him the nickname, "Hurry up" Yost. He was also an innovator of the [[hurry up offense]].{{cite web|url=http://www.soonersports.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=31000&ATCLID=208390369|title=Mossman: Hurry-Up Not New at OU}} ====Professional coach==== Yost initiated the concept of coaching as an actual profession near the turn of the century when he was paid as much as a UM professor. The professionalization of coaches that started with Yost and later, [[Walter Camp]] at [[Yale University]], symbolized how serious college football was becoming, and Yost symbolized this more so than any of his peers. It was he who first articulated the now accepted premise about student-athletes in the sport that: "Football builds character." ===Coaching tree=== No fewer than 77 men who either played for Yost, or coached under him as an assistant, went on to become head coaches in college football; two, [[Benny Friedman]] and [[Tommy Hughitt]], helmed teams in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).
